FR-106.title: Promise-aware annotator runner with explicit await
evidence: A-04 confirmed at engine.js:9093-9099 — _runAnnotator is sync (`try{return fn()}catch{...}`), does not await. 3 call sites pass async callbacks (annotateRuntimeCorrelation:9206, annotateFormalVerification:9216, annotatePathFeasibility:9221) whose rejections become unhandled and whose results can land after report construction.

Made engine.js's _runAnnotator Promise-aware: extracted its logic into scanner/src/pipeline/annotator-runner.js#runAnnotatorAsync (async, `return await fn()` inside the try — the crucial change, since `return fn()` without await let a rejected promise escape the catch entirely). engine.js's local _runAnnotator is now a one-line delegation closing over _annotatorErrors.

Added `await` to all 51 call sites of _runAnnotator in engine.js (verified via node --check, which would hard-fail on any await outside an async scope — proves every site is validly inside runFullScan's async body). Confirmed via grep that none of the 51 call sites capture _runAnnotator's return value (all mutate finalFindings via closure), so making every call awaited does not change execution order for the ~48 synchronous callbacks — only the 3 async ones (annotateRuntimeCorrelation, annotateFormalVerification, annotatePathFeasibility) change behavior: their work (and any rejection) now genuinely completes before runFullScan proceeds, instead of racing the return.

Confirmed via posture/CLAUDE.md that this codebase's own annotators are deliberately built never to throw ('no throwing' convention) — so there was no natural way to fault-inject a REAL annotator end-to-end. Extracted the logic into a standalone pure module specifically so the actual contract (reject -> captured, not unhandled; caller's await genuinely waits) could be fault-injection tested directly, rather than leaving FR-106's core claim unverified.
tests: test/annotator-runner.test.js (6 tests): sync value passthrough, async value passthrough+await, sync throw capture, ASYNC REJECTION capture with a live process 'unhandledRejection' listener proving it does NOT fire (the exact FR-106 regression case), await-actually-waits ordering proof, and independent-calls-dont-cross-contaminate.
Full npm test gate confirmed clean: 3986/3986 combined + 26/26 cpp-dataflow + python suites, exit 0. No regression from touching all 51 call sites in the core annotation pipeline.

FR-202.title: Real deadlines via worker/subprocess/interruptible execution
evidence: A-02 confirmed at engine.js:8498-8499 — per-file timeout is measured post-hoc (_ftElapsed>_perFileTimeoutMs) after the full synchronous detector chain already ran; not an interruptible deadline.

Cycle 66: D-0046 grounding investigation confirmed A-02's finding in more detail and extended it to deep-mode: engine.js's _perFileTimeoutMs (post-hoc, measured after the whole per-file detector chain already returned) and dataflow/engine.js's AGENTIC_SECURITY_DEEP_TIMEOUT_MS/deadlineMs (cooperative -- polls Date.now() every 128 worklist iterations, bounds only an already-bounded loop) are BOTH non-preemptive; a genuinely hung synchronous detector (infinite loop, catastrophic regex backtracking) is stopped by neither, since JavaScript is single-threaded and nothing in the same event loop can interrupt a synchronous hang. Found src/engine-parallel.js is dead, unwired scaffolding (AGENTIC_SECURITY_PARALLEL=1, zero real callers, its own header admits worker dispatch is deferred) -- a design sketch, not a working boundary. The outer loop now applies that delta to the shared arrays itself, exactly where the cascade used to mutate them directly; the two skip-continue checks (oversized file, dense file) and the checkpoint-replay early-continue were deliberately LEFT in the outer loop (not moved into the cascade) because moving them would have changed which iterations skip the trailing cooperative yield check -- a real behavioral subtlety found by reading the code closely rather than assumed away. _suppressionLog handling was deliberately NOT touched in 3a (it is written to transitively, deep inside 4 detectors' own internals, not at the top level of the cascade) -- converting those 4 detectors' suppression output to an explicit return value remains phase 3b's job, per D-0046's original checklist. FR-203.title: Per-file and per-analyzer coverage ledgers
evidence: Cycle 80 (D-0051): grounded FR-203 by auditing every one of _runFileCascade's ~130 detector call sites for their real applicability rules -- the direct prerequisite for a coverage ledger. Found: ~119 detectors run unconditionally (always applicable); 2 are file-extension-gated (scanRegexReDoS: java/cs/kt/py/php/phtml; scanGraphQL: graphql/gql); 9 are operator-policy-gated via individual AGENTIC_SECURITY_NO_* env vars nested inside a shared AGENTIC_SECURITY_NO_INTEGRATION gate (scanLlmApp, scanMobile, scanPqc, scanWeb3Advanced, scanDappFrontend, scanCloudIam, scanK8sAdmission, scanCryptoProtocol, scanMlSupplyChain) -- these map directly onto PRD section 10.2's named 'skipped_by_policy' status. Decided: FR-203 does NOT require refactoring every detector into a full AnalyzerResult-returning function (a much larger rewrite section 10.2 describes as the canonical shape, but which FR-201 itself -- already verified -- never implemented either, and which the literal FR-203 acceptance criterion does not demand). Instead: build a lightweight computeCoverageLedger(...) pure function over data ALREADY collected by FR-201/FR-202 -- _detectorErrors (name+file -> 'failed'), the file-timeout marker (-> 'timed_out' for every analyzer on that file, since a preemptive worker kill loses ALL in-flight analyzer state, not just one), the env-var gate table (-> 'skipped_by_policy', computed once per scan), the 2 extension gates (-> excluded from that file's ledger row entirely, not a 'skipped' status, since the PRD says 'every APPLICABLE analyzer'), and 'ran, didn't throw, file didn't time out' -> 'completed'. Mirrors D-0041/D-0046/D-0050's precedent: build the smallest correct primitive, test in isolation, wire into scan-health.js's currently-null 'analyzers' field as a separate step. NOT YET IMPLEMENTED -- this cycle was grounding only, per this session's established discipline of a dedicated grounding pass before large/architecturally-significant work. While grounding, found and fixed a real, unrelated FR-201 completeness gap (2 of 128 detector call sites -- scanWeb3Advanced/scanK8sAdmission -- were never wrapped in runDetector, a real violation of FR-201's own already-verified acceptance criterion); see FR-201's own evidence entry for full detail. Built src/pipeline/coverage-ledger.js: a static, verified-complete registry of all 121 runDetector-wrapped analyzer names extracted directly from engine.js's real cascade (cross-checked programmatically -- zero missing, zero extra), tagged by applicability (110 always, 2 extension-gated: scanRegexReDoS/scanGraphQL, 9 policy-gated via individual AGENTIC_SECURITY_NO_* env vars nested inside the shared AGENTIC_SECURITY_NO_INTEGRATION flag). computeCoverageLedger({files, detectorErrors, timedOutFiles, env}) computes, for every (file, applicable-analyzer) pair, exactly one terminal status -- completed/failed/timed_out/skipped_by_policy -- from data ALREADY produced by FR-201 (_detectorErrors) and FR-202 (the _timeout:true marker finding on a preemptively-killed file); an extension-gated analyzer not matching a file is EXCLUDED from that file's row entirely (not a status), matching the PRD's literal 'every APPLICABLE analyzer' wording. FR-204.title: Assurance modes: advisory, standard, strict
evidence: Cycle 83: implemented and wired FR-204 in full, building directly on FR-203's coverage ledger. Built src/pipeline/assurance-mode.js: a pure evaluateAssuranceMode(mode, scanHealth) function over the three named PRD modes (advisory/standard/strict). Advisory and standard are mechanically identical (never gate) since the PRD's own literal acceptance criterion only specifies strict mode's failure behavior -- inventing an intermediate mechanical distinction the PRD doesn't ask for was deliberately avoided. Strict mode fails when scan.scanHealth.status is not 'complete' -- covering all of the acceptance criterion's named cases (a failed/timed-out/silently-policy-skipped analyzer, via FR-203's coverage ledger; an annotator error or deep-mode failure, via FR-206's existing conditions) in one check, since scanHealth.status already aggregates every one of those signals. FR-208.title: Resumable execution invalidated by version/hash/policy change
evidence: Cycle 86: grounded first (per D-0014). scanner/src/posture/CLAUDE.md's own documentation said checkpoint invalidation was 'deliberately blunt' -- confirmed by reading scan-checkpoint.js directly: ONE run key hashed engine version, ruleset version, bundle SHA, EVERY scanned file's content, EVERY dependency-manifest file's content, and env switches into a single digest; any mismatch discarded the ENTIRE checkpoint (a test literally asserted this: 'changing a source file after the checkpoint discards it', with a comment reading 'this invalidates the whole checkpoint, not just that one entry'). This is the OPPOSITE of FR-208's literal acceptance criterion ('changed inputs invalidate ONLY AFFECTED checkpoints') -- a real, substantial gap, not a 'verify before assuming unbuilt' case like FR-205/FR-208-adjacent scan-checkpoint.js's own existence might have suggested.

Implemented genuine per-file granular invalidation without weakening the module's own stated correctness property ('a resumed scan must produce the same finding set as an uninterrupted one'). Split run identity into a GLOBAL key (engine version, ruleset version, bundle SHA, dependency-manifest contents, env switches -- computeGlobalKey()) and a PER-FILE content hash recorded on each checkpoint record. This split is architecturally sound, not a risk: per the module's own decision #2 ('only the per-file loop is checkpointed; every cross-file pass re-runs from scratch on resume'), a single scanned file's own per-file analysis result depends ONLY on that file's content plus the (now-separated) global identity -- nothing that changing a DIFFERENT file could affect. A global-identity change (engine/ruleset/bundle/deps/env) still discards the WHOLE checkpoint, unchanged from before, because those inputs affect every file's analysis.

'Record the invalidation reason' (the acceptance criterion's second half) implemented via a plaintext meta summary (globalKeyMeta()) stored alongside the opaque global key in the header -- used ONLY to explain a mismatch after the fact (_explainGlobalMismatch), never to decide one (the key comparison remains the sole source of truth, so a caller cannot bypass invalidation by supplying mismatched meta). A global discard now names exactly what changed (e.g. 'engine version changed (1.0.0 -> 2.0.0)', 'an AGENTIC_SECURITY_* environment switch changed'). A per-file discard is recorded via a new invalidatedFiles(handle) accessor, each entry naming the file and reason ('content changed since it was checkpointed' / 'no longer part of this scan'). Both surfaced on scan._scanMeta.checkpoint (new fields: discarded, discardReason, invalidatedFileCount, invalidatedFiles (bounded sample of 20), invalidatedFilesTruncated).

Checkpoint format bumped from /1 to /2 so a pre-existing on-disk /1 checkpoint (old semantics) can never be half-interpreted under the new per-file-aware format -- the safest possible migration (any old checkpoint is simply discarded once, matching the module's existing 'never resume into ambiguity' philosophy).

A record written without tracked file content (a handle opened without a fileContents map -- e.g. every pre-existing low-level protocol test in scan-checkpoint.test.js) is trusted exactly as before FR-208 (no per-file comparison possible, so none is attempted) -- this kept 9 of scan-checkpoint.test.js's existing low-level tests passing with only a mechanical runKey->globalKey parameter rename, zero behavior-assertion changes, since they test corruption/tamper/format mechanics orthogonal to per-file freshness.

Two existing END-TO-END tests DID need their asserted behavior changed, deliberately: 'changing a source file after the checkpoint discards it' and 'adding or removing a file discards the checkpoint' both asserted the OLD blunt behavior (resumed:0 after any file-set change) -- this is precisely the behavior FR-208 requires changing. Rewrote both (now 3 tests: change/add/remove) to assert the new, correct behavior using a real interrupted-then-resumed scan: changing one already-checkpointed file now resumes every OTHER already-checkpointed file and re-analyzes only the changed one, producing an IDENTICAL finding set to an uninterrupted baseline (proving the correctness property survives the granularity change, not just that resumed>0).

Both real entry points were ALREADY fail-closed before this cycle — FR-302's acceptance criterion was behaviorally satisfied.

Found the actual gap: FR-301's own apply-fix-service.js built a `readVerifiedScan()` function (docstring literally claims 'a caller ... MUST refuse the write') that had ZERO real callers anywhere in src/, bin/, or any test — confirmed via full-tree grep. Both CLI and MCP achieve the same fail-closed OUTCOME today, but only because each independently re-implements its own integrity check, not because the shared service enforces it. This is exactly the 'three independent copies of the same safety check' drift risk FR-301's own header comment names as the reason the service exists ('This module is the one place all of that lives now').

Wired `readVerifiedScan` into `applyVerifiedFix` itself as a defense-in-depth check, evaluated before path confinement, before verification, before any write — refuses with a distinct `integrity check failed: <status>` reason unless status is exactly 'verified'. This does not replace either caller's own pre-check (both still need the scan CONTENT to look up the finding by id, not just a pass/fail signal) — it protects any FUTURE caller of the shared service that forgets its own check, which is the actual security property 'one shared service' is supposed to guarantee.

Confirmed via 4 new direct unit tests (test/apply-fix-service.test.js) that call applyVerifiedFix directly, bypassing BOTH existing callers' pre-checks: missing last-scan.json -> refused ('missing'), no .sig -> refused ('unsigned'), tampered .sig -> refused ('tampered'), genuinely verified -> NOT refused by the integrity check (positive control). All 4 prove the shared service is safe on its own, not merely safe by caller convention.

FR-304.title: Fresh rescan proving original stable ID gone, no new policy-violating finding
evidence: Read posture/fix-verify.js's verifyPatch (called via applyVerifiedFix's verifyFixCore) in full before assuming scope: it ALREADY does a genuine fresh rescan every time it is called — runFullScan against the exact candidate content being written (not a cached/stale scan), checks the original finding's stableId is gone, and refuses if any new medium+ finding was introduced. Confirmed there is NO verification-result caching anywhere in the codebase (grepped for any store/reuse of a prior verify_fix verdict): every apply attempt, on every call path, always re-verifies fresh. This closes half of FR-304's acceptance criterion ('a fresh rescan proving the original stable ID is gone and no new finding violates policy') outright — it was already true, by construction, before this cycle.

Found the genuinely unaddressed half: 'a changed file invalidates approval'. verifyFixCore's rescan (plus lint/test legs when configured) takes real, measured wall-clock time (55ms-400ms+ even for a single trivial file, outside combined-suite load) during which the ON-DISK target file could be modified by something else — and nothing detected that. applyVerifiedFix's write step re-read the file fresh (for backup/diff purposes) but never compared it against what was on disk when verification STARTED, so a concurrent edit during that window was silently clobbered with no detection, no error, no audit trail distinguishing it from a normal apply.

Added hashFileContentSync + detectConcurrentModification to apply-fix-service.js: every confined file's content is hashed BEFORE verification starts; ALL files are re-hashed and compared against that baseline immediately before any write, refusing the ENTIRE batch (not partially writing some files before catching drift on a later one) if any file changed — covers both an existing file being edited AND a not-yet-existent file being concurrently created (both directions of 'changed').

Found and fixed a genuine TOCTOU in hashFileContentSync's own first draft (existsSync-then-readFileSync — the same bug class already fixed twice this session, in this same file's readVerifiedScan and in egress/policy.js's _loadPolicyConfig) via the self-scan gate, before the cycle closed — confirmed via direct code read, not assumed.

Deliberately did NOT test this via a wall-clock race against real verification timing — an isolated direct measurement showed 55ms vs 403ms for near-identical scenarios (10x variance even outside combined-suite load, the same resource-contention class as this session's own documented D-0006 flake), which would have made the test itself flaky. Instead extracted hashFileContentSync/detectConcurrentModification as pure, synchronous, directly-testable functions and proved the exact detection logic deterministically — 0.5-1ms per test, zero timing dependency, same functions applyVerifiedFix's real write path calls.

FR-306.title: Transactional write: backup, atomic replace, rollback, post-write hash
evidence: Read posture/fix-history.js's applyFix/undoLast/undoAll/recover in full before assuming scope (D-0003 discipline). Found real, genuine gaps against FR-306's literal wording: (1) the target-file write opened the path directly in truncate mode — a crash mid-write left a PARTIALLY-WRITTEN file, not an atomic replacement; (2) no post-write hash verification existed anywhere — a write that 'succeeded' (didn't throw) but produced wrong on-disk content (corrupting filesystem, truncated disk-full write, concurrent external modification) went completely undetected; (3) a failed write only recorded status:'failed' in the log — it never restored the target file, so a failed apply could leave a corrupted/partial file on disk indefinitely until someone manually noticed and ran `undo`; (4) a multi-file batch (the common case — most fixes touch one file, but the code path supports several) had NO cross-file rollback at all: if file 2 of 3 failed, file 1 stayed on its NEW content with no attempt to revert it.

Added _writeAtomicAndSync (temp-file-in-same-directory + fsync + rename, the standard atomic-replacement pattern; orphaned temp files cleaned up on any failure before the rename) and used it for both the backup write and the target-file write in applyFix.
Added post-write hash verification: after the atomic write, the file is read back and its hash compared against the intended content's hash before promoting the entry to 'applied'.

Added automatic single-file rollback: any failure in the write-then-verify step (write threw, OR verification caught a mismatch) now triggers an immediate restore — writes the original content back atomically if the file existed before, or deletes it if the fix had created a new file (added a `fileExisted` parameter threaded from both real callers, which already computed this via fs.existsSync — a naive 'always write original content back' would leave a phantom empty file where a new file never existed before, verified as a real distinct case via a dedicated test). Failure and rollback outcome are both recorded on the log entry: `error`in the log entry — the recoverable audit record — even when the restore itself also fails (recorded honestly as `rolledBack:false, restoreError` rather than silently claiming success).

Added multi-file batch rollback in BOTH real callers (apply-fix-service.js's applyVerifiedFix, mcp/tools.js's caller-patch branch): when a later file in a batch fails, every file the batch had ALREADY successfully written is rolled back via a new revertEntryById targeted-revert function, before the original error propagates — proving FR-306's literal acceptance criterion ('injected write failure restores all files') for the actual multi-file case, not just the single-file case applyFix already handled on its own.

Discovered and closed a genuine, PRE-EXISTING gap while in this code: undoLast/undoAll/the CLI `undo` command had ZERO test coverage anywhere in this codebase (confirmed via grep across every test file) despite being the write-reverting half of the fix pipeline. Refactored them to share the same _revertEntryInner primitive as the new revertEntryById (same atomic-write, same fileExisted-aware delete-vs-restore choice) and wrote 13 new direct tests (test/fix-history.test.js) — this session's now-established discipline of not leaving newly-touched, previously-uncovered code without tests.
Removed the now-dead writeLog helper (the old non-atomic, non-fsync log writer) after refactoring its one caller to use the existing _writeLogAndSync.

FR-307.title: Require human approval for high-impact change classes
evidence: Deliberately broke this session's repeated pattern of defaulting back to the E5/E6/E7/E8 survey and picked an entirely-unexamined epic instead (E3's remainder), per the handoff's own note that this deferral had repeated across 6+ cycles. Survey (D-0014 method) found posture/material-change.js already implements exactly the pattern-based diff-risk classifier FR-307 needs (auth-removed, priv-from-body, new-endpoint, new-iac-privilege, pipeline-perms-widened kinds already existed, built for a DIFFERENT purpose -- scoring a git PR diff for review triage) but is not wired into fix/apply-fix-service.js's write path at all, and its existing kind taxonomy did not yet cover 3 of the PRD's 7 named categories: crypto, PII, schema.

Extended material-change.js's ADD_PATTERNS with 3 new kinds covering the missing categories: weak-crypto-added/crypto-primitive-changed (md5/sha1/weak-cipher/JWT-signing usage), new-pii-field (reuses dataflow/privacy-taxonomy.js's FR-402 field-name vocabulary directly rather than inventing a second, parallel PII field-name list that could drift from the first), schema-change (DDL statements that alter or remove a table/column). Added an explicit HIGH_IMPACT_CATEGORY_OF_KIND map naming which `kind`s constitute one of the PRD's 7 named classes (auth, authZ, crypto, pii, schema, infra-privilege, public-api) -- a finding whose kind is not in this map still contributes to severity scoring as before but does not by itself trigger the approval gate.

Added classifyFixMaterialRisk(files) -- takes the SAME {relPath: {before, after}} content shape apply-fix-service.js already has on hand for every candidate write (no git invocation, no unified-diff text needed), builds a crude but sufficient line-set diff per file, and reuses the existing classifyHunk/summarize machinery unchanged. Wired into applyVerifiedFix() (fix/apply-fix-service.js): classification runs BEFORE verification (fail-fast, same reasoning FR-304's baseline-hash check already applies -- no point running a real rescan+lint+test pass on a candidate that will be refused regardless). When any finding's kind maps to a named high-impact category, the write is refused unless fixMeta.approval:{approvedBy, reason} is present with both fields non-empty -- a no-op for every OTHER candidate (the overwhelming majority of fixes), matching this codebase's restricts-nothing-until-triggered convention already used by egress/policy.js and dataflow/privacy-sink-policy.js.

Deliberately allows dryRun:true to preview PAST the gate without approval evidence (a dry run never writes anything -- applied is always false -- so blocking the preview itself would only prevent an agent from learning it needs to go collect approval before attempting a real apply, with no corresponding safety benefit). materialClassification is attached to every return path (refusal, dry-run preview, and successful apply) so the high-impact determination is never silent.

Proven end-to-end through the real applyVerifiedFix() call path, not the classifier in isolation: a test drives an actual auth-removal fix through the real service with skipVerification:true, confirms it is refused with zero bytes written to disk, confirms the SAME candidate succeeds once fixMeta.approval carries both required fields, confirms an approval object missing either field still fails the gate (no placeholder bypass), confirms an ordinary non-high-impact fix needs no approval at all, confirms dryRun previews without approval while never writing, and confirms PII/crypto/schema are each independently recognized end-to-end alongside auth.

CYCLE 44 CORRECTION (D-0024): while surveying FR-1003, found this gate was UNREACHABLE from both of its real production callers -- the MCP apply_fix tool's fixMeta inputSchema never declared an `approval` property (additionalProperties:false rejected any real caller supplying it, confirmed by direct execution against the schema validator), the MCP tool's OTHER branch (caller-supplied patch, the more commonly used path) never called applyVerifiedFix() at all and so had no high-impact gate whatsoever, and the CLI's fix --apply had no flag to ever supply approval evidence. All three fixed this cycle (schema property added; the same material-risk-classify-then-gate logic added to the patch branch; --approved-by/--approval-reason CLI flags added), with new tests proving reachability through the REAL MCP schema and REAL CLI subprocess, not applyVerifiedFix() called directly (which is what the original tests here proved, and is exactly why the gap was missed). See D-0024 for full detail.

FR-308.title: Record fix completeness and residual risk from mechanical evidence
evidence: Survey (D-0014 method) before building: posture/fix-honesty-gate.js already implements a FULL/MITIGATION/WORKAROUND tier classifier (computeFixTier) and a tier/residual consistency check (gateFixOutput), documented and tested. But the module's OWN header comment, and mcp/tools.js's own inline comments at both real call sites, already say plainly: 'the gate can only run against claims the AGENT self-reports... nothing here is server-computable.' The tier is entirely SELF-REPORTED (fixMeta.signals, an agent-supplied object) -- gateFixOutput only checks that a self-reported tier is INTERNALLY consistent with a self-reported residual, never that either reflects reality. FR-308's own title says 'from MECHANICAL evidence' -- the literal gap this cycle closes.

Identified the one piece of GENUINELY mechanical (server-computed, not agent-claimed) evidence already available in the real verification pipeline: fix-verify.js's PoC-execution leg (posture/CLAUDE.md's own execution-proof tiers) actually RUNS the finding's proof-of-concept against the candidate patch inside the sandbox and observes whether it still demonstrates the vulnerability -- a real fact, not a claim. Reused it rather than building a new mechanism.

Added checkMechanicalTierEvidence(tier, pocLeg) to fix-honesty-gate.js: when a self-reported tier is FULL but the PoC leg's status is still-exploitable, the claim is REFUTED (ok:false, a named violation), not merely internally-inconsistent. Deliberately narrow and one-directional: a non-FULL tier (MITIGATION/WORKAROUND) is UNAFFECTED by a still-exploitable PoC -- those tiers already honestly document a residual and are not claiming the flaw is fully closed, so a partially-working PoC against a MITIGATION is expected, not a violation. An inconclusive/not-requested/absent pocLeg is also a no-op -- this check can only ADD a violation on real contrary evidence, never manufacture one from absence of evidence.

Wired into fix-verify.js's verifyFix(): reordered the PoC leg to compute BEFORE the honesty gate (previously the honesty gate ran first and had no access to pocLeg at all), then passed the real pocLeg into gateFixOutput(fixMeta, {pocLeg}) as a new, backward-compatible optional second parameter (omitting it entirely -- the only call site before this cycle, and every existing test -- reproduces the exact prior self-consistency-only behavior). Both real MCP callers (apply_fix, verify_fix in mcp/tools.js) already call verifyFixCore with BOTH fixMeta AND poc together (confirmed by reading both call sites directly) -- so this fix reaches both real production callers with ZERO changes needed to mcp/tools.js or its input schemas.

Both axes are ADDITIVE constraints on the existing (class, sink) allow rule — a rule naming neither field behaves exactly as an FR-404 rule always did, proven by the full pre-existing FR-404 test suite (13 tests) passing unchanged after the extension.

Both new axes FAIL CLOSED: _matchesEnvironment/_matchesDestination return false (not true) when the rule declares a constraint but the caller supplied no matching context — an environment-scoped rule never silently applies to an unknown environment, and an invalid operator-supplied destination regex never silently matches everything. This mirrors the same fail-closed direction every other precision gate in this codebase takes when evidence is unavailable (per dataflow/CLAUDE.md's own stated convention for match.requireLiteralArg).

The environment value is resolved ONLY from an explicit opts.environment or the AGENTIC_SECURITY_ENVIRONMENT env var — deliberately NEVER from NODE_ENV, because this codebase's own sast/env-hygiene.js-adjacent detectors already flag NODE_ENV as "unreliable as a security boundary" for application code (engine.js's own Env-Gated Route finding), and the same reasoning applies to a scanner's own policy decisions: conflating a build-tool convention with a deployment-identity signal would make the axis silently wrong in exactly the situations it matters most (a bundler or test runner setting NODE_ENV=production for unrelated reasons).

FR-501.title: Six-state control evidence model replaces binary mapping
evidence: A-07 confirmed at auditor-walkthrough.js:294 — `scoped.filter(f => !f.intentSuppressed && !f.pastDecision && (f.severity==='critical'||f.severity==='high'))` is the only severity filter; medium findings never affect control satisfaction. NOTE: posture/privacy-framework.js is a SEPARATE, newer module implementing a 4-state (gap/engine-gap/manual/satisfied) model for NIST Privacy Framework specifically — auditor-walkthrough.js (the A-07 target) is an older, still-binary path used by other frameworks. FR-501's six-state model should generalize privacy-framework.js's pattern to auditor-walkthrough.js rather than building a third system.

Read posture/auditor-walkthrough.js in full (478 lines). Found it is FAR more sophisticated than the A-07 evidence table implied: already 4 statuses (present/partial/absent/manual), already caps codeTestable:'no'/'partial' controls below 'present', already handles unmapped-family disclosure (COMPLIANCE_FAMILY_GAPS) and unverifiable rule: mappings. The ACTUAL bug is narrow: the family: mapping's 'open finding' filter only counted severity critical/high (line ~294), so a control with any number of open MEDIUM findings on its mapped family rendered '✓ no open critical/high findings' — a vacuous pass, the exact failure mode privacy-framework.js's header comment already names ('the same false assurance... arriving by a different route').

Fixed: added a named SEVERITY_RANK + OPEN_FINDING_MIN_SEVERITY='medium' constant (not a policy config system — that's FR-502's fuller, separate scope) and changed the filter from `severity==='critical'||severity==='high'` to a rank comparison against the new floor. Deliberately did NOT lower the floor to 'low' (would make nearly every control partial, given how common low-severity findings are) — matches FR-502's own PRD wording distinguishing 'medium' from 'low' as the new baseline.

Built the deferred config surface: .agentic-security/compliance-severity-policy.json, read by a new _resolveOpenFindingMinSeverity(scanRoot, frameworkId) in auditor-walkthrough.js. Shape: {default: 'low', byFramework: {gdpr: 'low'}} -- byFramework wins over default, default overrides the built-in 'medium' floor for every framework with no more specific entry, and an unrecognized/malformed value ALWAYS falls back to the safe 'medium' default rather than reaching the SEVERITY_RANK lookup with an invalid key (which would silently make the >= comparison always false, treating every finding as not-open -- the exact vacuous-pass bug this whole threshold exists to prevent). FR-503.title: Require positive evidence for satisfaction where the control demands implementation proof
evidence: Survey (D-0014 method): confirmed compliance-policy.js's file-exists/documented primitive treats mere existence as sufficient, with no way for a mapping author to demand the file's CONTENT prove something -- matching the acceptance criterion's literal gap ('mere artifact existence... is insufficient UNLESS the mapping explicitly defines it').

Built a NEW, additive verifier primitive, file-contains: {path, pattern}, rather than changing file-exists's default behavior -- file-exists remains fully valid for controls that genuinely only need a document to exist (e.g. 'an incident response PLAN exists'); file-contains is what a mapping author opts INTO for a control that demands positive content proof (e.g. 'a CI workflow that actually configures dependency automation', not merely a file named that way). This is the literal reading of 'insufficient UNLESS the mapping explicitly defines it' -- the mapping now has a way to explicitly define stronger proof, without weakening the existing, already-correct behavior of the primitive that came before it.

Deliberately did NOT attempt to audit or upgrade the bundled compliance framework JSON files (nist-privacy-1-1.json, hipaa-security-rule.json, etc.) to decide which existing file-exists-mapped controls SHOULD be upgraded to file-contains -- that is real, separate, fuzzy-scoped curation work (deciding, framework by framework, which controls genuinely demand implementation proof vs. mere existence), left honestly as future work per D-0020's discipline for a multi-part gap. FR-504.title: Bind conclusions to repository, commit, scope, engine, ruleset, analyzer health, and mapping version
evidence: Survey (D-0014 method): confirmed two distinct compliance-evidence-producing modules exist -- posture/auditor-walkthrough.js (framework/family-mapping evaluator, FR-501/502's own scope) and posture/compliance-policy.js (the customer-DSL 'compliance-as-code' evaluator whose OWN header already says its output is 'consumable by Vanta/Drata/SecureFrame/auditors' -- external GRC tooling, matching FR-508's own wording, and confirmed as in-scope for this epic since FR-507's evidence-grade-wording fix already touched it). Built computeEvidenceDigest(fields) -- a sha256 of an explicit ALLOWLIST {repository, commit, scope, engine, ruleset, analyzerHealth, mappingVersion, controls[{id,status}]}, deterministic-JSON-then-hash, mirroring attestation.js's own canonicalisation shape exactly rather than inventing a fourth scheme in this codebase (this session's now-repeated discipline, D-0023/D-0025/D-0026). Wired into verifyPolicy() itself so every real caller gets a digest automatically -- commit is auto-resolved via `git rev-parse HEAD` (new _currentCommit helper, degrading to null off-git, matching sbom-diff.js's own established pattern for the same lookup) when not explicitly supplied by the caller; analyzerHealth reads ctx.scanHealth?.status (FR-206's own signal) when the caller supplies it.

Proven end-to-end: the digest is present and correctly shaped on every real verifyPolicy() call; identical inputs produce an identical digest (deterministic, not a fresh random id); EACH of repository/commit/ruleset/analyzerHealth/mappingVersion/control-outcome changing independently changes the digest (6 separate assertions, not one combined smoke test); control array ORDER does not change the digest (sorted before hashing, same discipline as attestation.js's own sorted-canonicalisation). FR-505.title: Sign evidence manifests when signing is configured
evidence: Built scanner/src/posture/compliance-evidence-signing.js, reusing evidence-bundle.js's Ed25519 keypair VERBATIM (ensureKeyPair/keyPaths, no new key directory) rather than a third or fourth key domain -- a compliance evidence manifest and a finding evidence bundle make the SAME kind of claim (self-attestation by the running install that an artifact is exactly what it produced), unlike policy-bundle.js's org-authored/distributed trust domain (D-0026's own distinction, applied correctly rather than defaulted-to-copy).

Applied D-0026's EA-03 lesson from the FIRST write, not discovered later: canonicalComplianceEvidenceBytes signs an explicit allowlist covering EVERY key emitEvidenceJsonLd() can actually produce, and verifyComplianceEvidence REJECTS any top-level key outside {that allowlist, signature} -- proven directly by a test stapling an extra field onto a validly-signed document.

Chose to sign the FULL rendered document (framework/version/generatedAt/disclaimer/provenance/evidenceDigest/summary/controls[[with checks+narrative_evidence]]), not just FR-504's own narrower evidenceDigest (which binds only {id,status} per control) -- FR-505's acceptance criterion ('altered findings, scope, POLICY, OR EVIDENCE REFERENCES') is broader than 'the conclusion changed', and a test proves this distinction concretely: editing a control's narrative_evidence bullet (unchanged status) is caught by the full-document signature but would NOT have been caught by evidenceDigest alone.

'WHEN SIGNING IS CONFIGURED' implemented as a genuine no-op-until-opted-in, not an auto-generate-on-first-use behavior (deliberately DIFFERENT from `agentic-security attest`'s own auto-generate default): built loadSigningKeyIfConfigured(), which only ever READS an existing key (read-first-in-try/catch, D-0012) and never generates one. Rationale recorded in the function's own header: compliance evidence is emitted automatically on every ordinary scan, so silently creating key material as a side effect of a routine scan would be surprising and unrequested, unlike an explicit `attest` invocation where auto-generation is the right default. Wired into emitEvidenceJsonLd(): unsigned when no key exists (the common case, proven unchanged/backward-compatible), signed when an operator has already configured one (e.g. by running `attest` once).

Extended the existing `verify-attestation` CLI command to auto-detect a compliance evidence manifest (@type: ComplianceEvidence) as a THIRD recognizable shape, alongside its existing run-attestation and finding-evidence-bundle detection -- reusing one operator-facing verification entry point rather than adding a fourth CLI command for the same underlying question ('is this artifact exactly what was signed').

Proven end-to-end through the REAL CLI, not the library functions in isolation: a real compliance evidence file signed with a real generated keypair verifies successfully via `agentic-security verify-attestation <file> --public-key <path>` (prints framework/version/digest/summary), and a subsequently-tampered copy of the SAME file is correctly rejected as INVALID through the same command.
tests: scanner/test/compliance-evidence-signing.test.js (new, 13 tests): sign+verify round trip, wrong-key rejection, 2 distinct tamper-detection tests (control status changed; narrative_evidence changed with status UNCHANGED -- the test that specifically proves signing covers more than FR-504's digest), EA-03 stapled-key rejection, unsigned-document rejection, no-public-key-supplied graceful rejection, canonical-bytes key-order independence, loadSigningKeyIfConfigured's no-key/has-key behavior (via a redirected XDG_CONFIG_HOME, never touching the real user key directory), emitEvidenceJsonLd's unsigned-by-default and signed-when-configured behavior (both through the real function, confirming the ON-DISK artifact is the signed version), and a real CLI round trip (sign -> write -> verify-attestation succeeds -> tamper -> verify-attestation fails).

Full existing compliance-policy.js suite (world-class-batch2.test.js's 8 tests, compliance-evidence-binding.test.js's 18 tests) re-run unchanged and green -- confirms signing is purely additive and does not alter any existing verdict or unsigned-mode behavior.

FR-506.title: Add evidence freshness, owner, reviewer, exception, and expiry
evidence: Extended compliance-policy.js's DSL with 5 new optional, additive per-control fields (owner, reviewer, reviewed-at, review-interval-days, and a richer structured `not-applicable` form) -- a control naming none of these is completely unaffected, matching this session's established no-op-until-configured convention for every gate built this session.

FRESHNESS: a control opting into review-interval-days becomes status 'stale' once reviewed-at (or, if never set, treated as maximally stale from the start -- not a free pass) exceeds the configured interval. Staleness is checked AFTER the real compliant/non-compliant verdict and can only ever downgrade an otherwise-COMPLIANT control -- a control already failing its checks does not need a second, redundant 'also old' caveat.

EXCEPTION/EXPIRY: extended the existing bare-boolean `not-applicable: true` (kept working forever, unchanged, for the many existing policy YAMLs using it) to ALSO accept a structured object `{reason, owner, expires-at}`. An EXPIRED structured exception reopens the control as a NEW status, `gap` -- not silently falling back to whatever `requires` would have said, since the underlying checks were never actually run under an exception. This is the literal 'expired... exception changes status to stale or gap' acceptance criterion, split cleanly: expired EVIDENCE -> stale, expired EXCEPTION -> gap.

owner/reviewer are carried through as plain accountability metadata into both the JSON-LD (compliance-evidence.json) and markdown (compliance-evidence.md) artifacts, present only when set -- no fabricated accountability for the overwhelming majority of controls that name neither.

Summary counts (compliant/nonCompliant/notApplicable) extended with stale/gap, reported at the TOP LEVEL of the summary object, not buried inside individual controls -- a summary reporting 'compliant: 40' while 5 of those are stale evidence or 3 are gaps hiding behind expired exceptions is exactly the false-assurance shape this PRD item exists to close.
tests: scanner/test/compliance-evidence-binding.test.js (12 of its 18 tests are FR-506-specific): review-interval-exceeded becomes stale with a staleReason; reviewed-within-interval stays compliant; no-interval-configured is never stale regardless of how old reviewed-at is; a non-compliant control is never double-flagged stale; a legacy bare not-applicable:true never expires; a structured exception with a past expires-at reopens as gap (and is NOT double-counted as not-applicable); a structured exception with a future expires-at stays not-applicable; owner/reviewer render in both artifacts when set and are absent (not fabricated) when unset; direct _staleness/_exceptionExpired unit tests via _internals.
Full gate: same run as FR-504 above (npm test 4473/4473, corpus 215/215, self-scan zero drift, build clean, smoke exit 3).
FR-506.remainingWork: None for this requirement's stated acceptance criterion. Not built: any AUTOMATED reminder/notification when a control is approaching staleness or exception expiry (the acceptance criterion asks for the STATUS to change, which it does, not for proactive alerting) -- a real, separate future enhancement if ever requested.

FR-507.title: Replace certification-style wording with evidence-grade wording
evidence: Investigation (continuing the E5/E7/E8/E9 survey the FR-704 cycle recommended) found 4 independently hand-rolled compliance disclaimers across the codebase, already drifted from each other: compliance-policy.js (2 occurrences), auditor-walkthrough.js, privacy-framework.js, and report/oscal.js. A REAL, CONFIRMED terminology bug: 3 of the 4 said some form of "a licensed assessor is responsible for the final attestation" — this gets the PRD's own three-tier vocabulary BACKWARDS. A licensed/accredited assessor produces an INDEPENDENT CERTIFICATION (or an assessment opinion), not a management attestation; an ATTESTATION is specifically the organization's OWN leadership formally asserting that controls are in place and operating (the SOC 2 "management assertion" model). docs/OSCAL.md's own prose ("It is not an attestation that the control is implemented and operating") already used the term correctly, but report/oscal.js's actual emitted remarks field never named "independent certification" as a distinct term either — the acceptance criterion ("UI and docs distinguish automated technical assessment, management attestation, and independent certification") asks for all THREE tiers named explicitly, not just a generic 'not certified' caveat.

scanner/src/posture/evidence-grade-wording.js (new): single canonical source of truth. ASSURANCE_TIERS names and defines all three tiers distinctly (automated technical assessment = what this tool produces; management attestation = the organization's own leadership's job, which this tool cannot do; independent certification = an accredited third party's job, which this tool also cannot do). EVIDENCE_GRADE_DISCLAIMER (full, for machine-consumed/structured fields) and EVIDENCE_GRADE_DISCLAIMER_SHORT (for markdown blockquotes) both name all three tiers explicitly while preserving the exact substring 'does not certify compliance' that 2 pre-existing tests (CMP-5, world-class-batch2.test.js) already pinned — proven unbroken by running those tests unchanged after the wording swap, not by updating them to match.

All 4 call sites now reference the shared module instead of hand-rolling: compliance-policy.js's emitEvidenceJsonLd disclaimer field and emitEvidenceMarkdown blockquote; privacy-framework.js's markdown blockquote (was previously a 2-line disclaimer that never named either tier by name, just said 'it does not certify anything' and 'a licensed assessor is responsible for the attestation'); auditor-walkthrough.js's renderWalkthrough blockquote (removed the exact backwards phrasing); report/oscal.js's toOSCALCompliance remarks field (kept 'No licensed assessor reviewed this document' — an OSCAL-specific, correctly-directional fact — appended after the shared full disclaimer, rather than reinventing a 5th variant).

Deliberately did NOT touch posture/attestation.js or posture/evidence-bundle.js's naming — those implement a completely different, unrelated concept (per-install symmetric-HMAC / Ed25519 cryptographic tamper-evidence for run/finding data, an already well-scoped Milestone-2 feature) that happens to share the English word 'attestation' with the PRD's compliance-tier vocabulary. Renaming a working, already-tested feature to avoid a word collision would be scope creep unjustified by FR-507's actual acceptance criterion, which is about compliance-evidence-facing UI/docs wording specifically.
tests: scanner/test/evidence-grade-wording.test.js (new, 8 tests): ASSURANCE_TIERS names all three tiers distinctly; both disclaimer variants name all three tiers AND preserve the pre-existing 'does not certify compliance' substring AND assert the old backwards phrasing is GONE (assert.doesNotMatch), not just supplemented; each of the 4 real call sites (compliance-policy.js's JSON-LD field verbatim-equality, its markdown embed, oscal.js's toOSCALCompliance remarks, privacy-framework.js's persisted markdown, auditor-walkthrough.js's renderWalkthrough) is individually proven to carry the shared wording through its REAL public entry point, not a mocked/synthetic call.

Pre-existing tests proven unbroken, not updated to match: the 2 CMP-5 tests in world-class-batch2.test.js (world-class-batch2.test.js, compliance-policy: emitEvidenceJsonLd/emitEvidenceMarkdown carry the disclaimer) pass unchanged — confirming the exact substring they pin survived the wording upgrade. Full oscal-conformance.test.js (all remarks-field assertions target OTHER observation records, not the one touched) and privacy-framework.test.js both pass unchanged.

npm run test:posture: 1776/1776 (1768 + 8 new). npm run test:report: 250/250 (unchanged — oscal-conformance.test.js lives in test:posture, confirmed by direct grep before assuming scope). npm run test:lifecycle: 248/248 + command-description-lint clean (dead-module guard confirms evidence-grade-wording.js's exports are genuinely imported by all 4 call sites).

If a future module emits a compliance-adjacent disclaimer, it should import from evidence-grade-wording.js rather than hand-rolling a 5th variant — there is no automated guard preventing that recurrence (unlike, say, the write-seam guard for state-dir.js), so this is worth a note for whoever adds the next compliance-artifact emitter.

FR-508.title: Export evidence in a stable API suitable for external GRC ingestion
evidence: Survey: the acceptance criterion is concrete, not vague -- 'exported records retain source references, status semantics, and schema version.' Confirmed the existing compliance-evidence.json JSON-LD artifact (now signed per FR-505) had NONE of the three explicitly: the @vocab URL embedded an implicit '/v1/' with no machine-readable version field; no status value's meaning was documented anywhere in the artifact itself; no per-export pointer named which policy file produced it.

Added 3 fields to emitEvidenceJsonLd()'s output, all additive: schemaVersion (a plain integer, exported as EVIDENCE_SCHEMA_VERSION -- a real number a consumer checks programmatically, separate from the URL-embedded version string), statusSemantics (an exported STATUS_SEMANTICS dictionary defining what each of the 5 real status values -- compliant/non-compliant/not-applicable/stale/gap -- actually means, so a GRC tool ingesting this artifact does not need to reverse-engineer this codebase's own source to interpret a status string), and policySource (the relative path to the compliance.policy.yml that produced this specific export -- the one per-export source reference not already implicit in each control's own checks[].rule).

Documented the version-bump discipline explicitly in EVIDENCE_SCHEMA_VERSION's own comment: every field this session has added to this artifact (evidenceDigest, owner/reviewer/staleReason/gapReason, signature, and now these 3) was optional and backward-compatible, which IS the stability guarantee FR-508 asks for -- bump only when an EXISTING field's meaning changes incompatibly, not for a genuinely additive field.

Kept compliance-evidence-signing.js's (FR-505) EA-03-safe allowlist in sync with the 3 new fields, per that module's own documented obligation -- proven by 2 new tests confirming tampering with schemaVersion or statusSemantics after signing is detected, exactly like every other signed field.

Found and fixed a real violation of this codebase's own state-path discipline while implementing: test/no-stray-state.test.js correctly caught a hardcoded '.agentic-security/' string literal in the new policySource field (a DISPLAY string, not an actual file operation, but the guard's detector does not distinguish the two -- by design, since 'the seam' is meant to be the single place this name lives). Fixed properly, not worked around: exported the existing private STATE_DIR_NAME constant from state-dir.js and consumed it, rather than adding an ALLOWLIST exemption (which the guard's own error message explicitly says is not the fix).
tests: scanner/test/compliance-evidence-binding.test.js (+1 test): schemaVersion/statusSemantics/policySource all present and traced back to the module's own exported constants (not re-asserted as independent literals, proving the emitted document cannot silently drift from the single source of truth); every one of the 5 real status values confirmed to have a real, non-placeholder definition.
scanner/test/compliance-evidence-signing.test.js (+2 tests): tampering with schemaVersion or statusSemantics after signing is detected, extending FR-505's own EA-03 coverage to the 3 new fields.

A first full npm test run correctly caught the state-path-seam violation (test/no-stray-state.test.js) — fixed by exporting STATE_DIR_NAME from state-dir.js rather than an allowlist exemption; re-verified clean on a second full run.

Full gate, every exit code captured directly: npm test exit 0 (4500/4500 main suite + 26/26 cpp-dataflow + 1/1 fault-injection + python suites), bench:cve-replay:check exit 0 (215/215, zero drift), bench:self-scan:check exit 0 (scanner/src 436/436, zero drift -- the new fields and the STATE_DIR_NAME export introduced zero new self-flagged patterns), npm run build exit 0 (zero new untracked dist chunks), npm run smoke exit 3 (expected).

Not built: a separate, human-facing schema DOCUMENT (e.g. a markdown page describing the JSON-LD shape) -- the chosen design deliberately makes the artifact self-describing instead (schema version + status semantics travel WITH every export), which is more robust than separate documentation that can drift out of sync, and satisfies the literal 'exported records retain...' wording without inventing an additional maintenance burden.

FR-601.title: Egress policy evaluated before prompt construction and network access
evidence: A-09 confirmed at discovery/lenses.js:32 — DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS=60_000, raw file contents sliced directly into prompt with only a length truncation; grep for redact|policy in discovery/*.js returns zero matches.

Full audit (dispatched research pass) found the real scope was larger than A-09's single evidenced site: 7 distinct fetch() call sites across 6 files, in 4 independent code paths, with only 2 pre-existing shared chokepoints (discovery/llm-invoke.js for hunter.js+disprove.js; llm-validator/providers.js+index.js for the validator). adversary-agent.js, llm-redteam.js, flow-narration.js, and sca/llm-function-extract.js each had their own inline fetch with zero shared infrastructure — the same 'scattered append sites' shape as FR-101-104's canonical-pipeline problem.

Built scanner/src/egress/policy.js: evaluateEgress(ctx) — a real allow/deny decision evaluated by callers BEFORE prompt construction. Denial conditions implemented this cycle: AGENTIC_SECURITY_EGRESS_DENY=1 (blunt kill switch, mirrors the existing AGENTIC_SECURITY_LLM_VALIDATE=0 precedent), AGENTIC_SECURITY_EGRESS_MODE=deny / mode: deny in .agentic-security/egress-policy.yml, mode: local-only (reuses llm-validator/local-endpoint.js's isLoopbackUrl — literal-loopback-only, no DNS trust, no new logic duplicated), and allowedProviders/deniedProviders lists. Default (no config, no env) is 'allow', preserving every existing LLM-backed feature's current default-on behavior — FR-601 asks for a policy DECISION on every call, not a policy that silently disables features nobody configured it to disable. Decision object is deliberately metadata-only (allowed, decision, reason, provider, policySource, purpose) — never carries prompt/source content, per the PRD walkthrough's scenario 7 ('records a sanitized decision without retaining source').

Wired all 7 call sites through evaluateEgress, each gated BEFORE its prompt-building code runs (verified per-site: discovery/llm-invoke.js's resolveLlmInvokeWithDecision resolves the decision before returning a callable, so hunter.js/disprove.js never build a prompt for a denied endpoint; llm-validator/index.js's validateOne gates immediately after endpointConfig() resolves, before renderPrompt(); adversary-agent.js gates before selecting defaultLlmInvoke; llm-redteam.js's runActiveRedteam gates once for the whole batch before any corpus prompt is sent; flow-narration.js's _renderLlm gates before building its template string; sca/llm-function-extract.js's extractVulnFunctionsViaLLM gates before its batch loop).

Threaded scanRoot through discovery/index.js's runHunter/disprovePanel call sites (previously only llmInvoke was forwarded, so config-file-based policy could not resolve the right .agentic-security/ directory for the real CLI `hunt` path) — found and fixed as part of wiring, not a separate FR.

Built a completeness-guard test (test/egress-policy-completeness.test.js) directly analogous to FR-701's artifact-registry-completeness.test.js: scans every fetch( call site under src/, requires each to either import evaluateEgress or be on a reviewed, justified EXCLUDED_FILES list (16 entries, each with a one-line reason — SCA/OSV registries, PoC harnesses that call the SCANNED app rather than a model, ticket/webhook integrations, Sigstore's Rekor log, and files where fetch( appears only in a comment). This is the anti-drift mechanism for exactly the scattered-call-site problem the initial audit found — a NEW LLM call site added later without gating now fails this test.

Fixed a genuine TOCTOU (existsSync-then-readFileSync race) in policy.js's own _loadPolicyConfig, found by the self-scan gate scanning the module's own source — same bug class, same fix pattern (read-first, catch ENOENT) already applied to fix/apply-fix-service.js earlier in this session.

Self-scan gate reviewed 3 drifts before accepting into baseline: egress/policy.js 0→1 (one expected low-severity dos-sync-io finding on new code, consistent with the same finding class already present across many other posture modules); integrations/index.js 10→11 (file confirmed byte-identical via git stash/diff — the +1 is a whole-tree cross-file detector's count shifting due to the total scanned tree composition changing, not a defect in the unchanged file, confirmed deterministic via 2 repeated scans); posture/flow-narration.js 3→1 (a genuine, expected reduction — the added egress gate's early-return changes control flow ahead of the fetch call, the same 'security fix legitimately reduces the scanner's own finding count on itself' pattern already seen with FR-804's risk-dollars.js fix).

Found and corrected a self-inflicted mistake during verification: a bulk `find test/fixtures -type d -name .agentic-security -prune -exec rm -rf +` cleanup (needed because 66+ fixture directories had accumulated stray, gitignored scan state from earlier npm run smoke/full-suite runs, corrupting 'no prior scan' tests) also deleted 2 GIT-TRACKED fixture files (test/fixtures/custom-rules/.agentic-security/rules.yml, test/fixtures/sca-suppression/.agentic-security/rules.yml). Caught by the very next full gate run, root-caused via `git status --short` showing tracked-file deletions, restored via `git checkout --`. Documented in decisions.md D-0009 with a standing lesson for future bulk cleanups in this tree. This same investigation also found and corrected the true root cause of decision D-0007's previously-unexplained 'no prior scan' test failures — not an undiagnosed code bug as originally concluded, but the identical stray-fixture-state mechanism (git stash cannot remove gitignored untracked files, which is why D-0007's stash-based falsification never found it).

Full verification gate run 2026-08-24 (after the TOCTOU fix): npm test 4091/4091 + 26/26 (cpp-dataflow/python), zero failures — not even a D-0006 flake this run. bench:cve-replay:check: 215/215, zero drift. bench:self-scan:check: clean after the 3 reviewed drifts above, baseline updated. npm run build: clean. npm run smoke: exit 3 (correctly reflects the 3 critical / 9 high findings the deliberately-vulnerable fixture is designed to trigger — matches this codebase's own `status <= 3` pass convention used throughout the test suite, not a failure).

test/egress-policy-integration.test.js (7 tests): for EACH of the 7 wired call sites, stubs global.fetch and proves a denied policy produces ZERO fetch calls (the literal FR-601 acceptance criterion) plus the expected degrade signal at that site (hunter degraded+reason, disprove undecided, validator's distinct egress-policy-denied error tag, adversary-agent's unverified-no-llm-endpoint outcome, llm-redteam's thrown error, flow-narration's template fallback, sca-llm-function-extract's empty-array degrade).

FR-602.title: Support provider, model, role, region, repository, path, data class, and maximum-context constraints
evidence: FR-601's own module header explicitly named this as deferred scope ("Deliberately NOT in scope here: the fuller constraint-dimension set — role/region/repository/path/data-class/max-context — FR-602"), and FR-601 had already built exactly ONE genuine, testable dimension (provider, via allowedProviders/deniedProviders). This cycle extends the SAME mechanism to the remaining 7 named dimensions rather than building a parallel system.

scanner/src/egress/policy.js: evaluateEgress(ctx) gained model/role/region/repository/path/dataClass/contextTokens as new OPTIONAL ctx fields. Design principle applied uniformly: each dimension is evaluated ONLY when the CALLER supplies the corresponding context value AND the config restricts that specific dimension — a caller with no opinion on, say, region must never be blocked by a region rule it has no way to satisfy or violate. This is the same default-open-unless-both-sides-opt-in shape provider already used, extended rather than reinvented. model/role/region/repository/dataClass use list-membership (allowedX/deniedX arrays, driven by a single LIST_DIMENSIONS table so the 5 near-identical checks share one code path rather than 5 copy-pasted blocks); path uses glob matching via util/glob.js's existing matchesAnyGlob (already used elsewhere in this codebase for ignore-pattern matching, reused rather than reimplemented) since a literal string is the wrong shape for a file-path constraint; maxContextTokens is a numeric cap compared against a caller-supplied ESTIMATE (evaluateEgress runs before prompt construction, so it has no prompt to measure itself — the caller must estimate).

Proven this is not purely theoretical: threaded role ('validate') and model (cfg.model) through llm-validator/index.js's real evaluateEgress call site — the SAME caller FR-601/605/606 already used as a real, wired proof point — so a deniedModels rule genuinely reaches the real validateOne() call path, verified end-to-end (a real deniedModels config blocks the actual fetch, not just the policy function in isolation).

local-only mode's own denial (FR-605) is confirmed to still take precedence over every new dimension — a remote endpoint is denied even when every other configured constraint (model/role/region) would independently allow it, and a loopback endpoint that ALSO satisfies every other configured dimension is correctly allowed. Multiple dimensions supplied together on one call are proven to require ALL of them to pass (a single failing dimension denies the whole call, not just that one aspect).

FR-604.title: Record per-call audit metadata without retaining prohibited prompt content
evidence: FR-601 gives every outbound LLM call a machine-readable IN-MEMORY decision object; the acceptance criterion asks for more -- a PERSISTED per-call record with purpose/provider/model/region/byte-token-counts/policy/hashes/outcome, WITHOUT retaining the prohibited prompt content. Surveyed for existing infrastructure first (D-0014 method): src/mcp/audit.js already implements exactly this class of guarantee for MCP tool calls -- an append-only NDJSON log where each entry's `prev` is the SHA-256 of the previous line, so tampering breaks the chain from that point forward (OWASP MCP08). Its own public API (`auditCall({tool, args, outcome})`) and internal hash-chain helpers are private/unexported and shaped around {tool,args}, not egress's {purpose,provider,model,region,policy,hashes} -- reshaping that already-tested, security-relevant module to export shared primitives was judged a separate refactor, out of proportion to one FR cycle, so the ~15-line hash-chain idiom (a single sha256 call) was deliberately mirrored rather than imported, with the reasoning recorded in the new module's own header comment.

Built scanner/src/egress/audit.js: `recordEgressCall({scanRoot, decision, ctx, metrics})` appends one NDJSON entry to `.agentic-security/egress-audit.log` per evaluateEgress() decision, and `payloadMetrics(text)` computes {byteCount, tokenCount (same Math.ceil(len/4) estimate llm-validator/index.js's own R12 cost ceiling already uses), contentHash} from an outbound payload WITHOUT ever returning or logging the text itself -- verified directly: JSON.stringify(payloadMetrics(secret)) does not contain the secret. A denied call (no payload ever built, by FR-601's own design -- evaluateEgress runs BEFORE prompt construction) is logged with byteCount/tokenCount/contentHash all null, which is correct: there is nothing to measure for a call that was never assembled.

Wired into the real, already-established caller: llm-validator/index.js's validateOne(). The deny branch (right after evaluateEgress returns not-allowed) records purpose/provider/model/policy/outcome/reason immediately. The allow branch records AFTER renderPrompt() builds the final, already-redacted (FR-603) prompt string -- the only point where a real byte count/token estimate/content hash actually exist -- using payloadMetrics(prompt) so the entry carries real metrics without ever persisting the prompt text.

Proven end-to-end through the real call path, not the module in isolation: an integration test drives validateOne() twice (once denied via a real `mode: deny` egress-policy.yml, once allowed with a finding whose file content contains a live secret), reads the actual .agentic-security/egress-audit.log file both times, and asserts: outcome/purpose/provider on the deny entry with byteCount=null; outcome=allow with real byteCount/tokenCount/contentHash on the second; the two entries chain (prev of entry 2 matches sha256 of entry 1's line); and the raw log FILE TEXT never contains the secret value that was in the validated finding's prompt. verifyEgressAuditLog() independently confirms the 2-entry chain is intact.

A proactive self-scan of the new module (npm run's own AGENTIC_SECURITY_DEEP invocation, before the full gate) surfaced a real, genuine defect before it was ever run through CI: verifyEgressAuditLog() was first written with the SAME existsSync()-then-readFileSync() TOCTOU pattern mcp/audit.js's own verifyAuditLog() already has (mirrored deliberately, per the design note above) -- but this session's own D-0012 discipline says every NEW reader should be read-first-in-try/catch from the start, so rather than accept the same latent pattern mcp/audit.js still carries, verifyEgressAuditLog was fixed to read-first before landing (2 TOCTOU findings -> 0, confirmed by re-running the self-scan directly). The remaining 1 finding (Synchronous Blocking I/O) matches the same accepted pattern already baselined for mcp/audit.js and other short-lived state-writer modules -- legitimate, not fixed.

FR-605.title: Enforce an unambiguous local-only provider mode
evidence: Investigation (continuing the E5/E7/E8/E9 survey) traced EVERY one of the 12 files in the codebase that reference AGENTIC_SECURITY_LLM_ENDPOINT directly, to determine whether mode:local-only is genuinely enforced for every real network-egress caller, not just the ones already known to be wired. 4 references were false positives (comments/error-message text only, no real call). 2 (posture/auditor-agent.js, posture/defender-agent.js) never construct their own HTTP client at all — they exclusively accept an injected opts.llmInvoke(transcript) callback with no endpoint/URL concept, correctly out of FR-605's scope (there is no URL to smuggle through an opaque callback the module never dials out through itself; the module's OWN default path, when it has one, is what needs gating, and both of these have none). 1 (discovery/hunter.js) correctly delegates through discovery/llm-invoke.js's resolveLlmInvokeWithDecision wrapper rather than calling evaluateEgress directly.

REAL, CONFIRMED-BY-EXECUTION GAP found: discovery/llm-invoke.js's OWN comment already flagged it as open ("Consensus mode (multiple endpoints) is NOT yet egress-filtered per endpoint... documented as explicit future scope, not silently skipped") — resolveLlmInvokeWithDecision's multi-endpoint branch (AGENTIC_SECURITY_LLM_ENDPOINTS, comma-separated) constructed its consensus caller with ZERO egress check, while the single-endpoint branch immediately below it DID call evaluateEgress. This meant mode:local-only was silently bypassable: an operator configuring local-only expecting every LLM call to stay on-machine would have every call blocked via the single-endpoint path, but a consensus list of remote URLs (e.g. AGENTIC_SECURITY_LLM_ENDPOINTS=https://api.openai.com/...,https://api.anthropic.com/...) would sail through completely ungated — the exact 'remote URL smuggled into local-only configuration' scenario FR-605's acceptance criterion names.

Fix: makeConsensusInvoke now evaluates evaluateEgress for EACH endpoint in the list individually before including it — a policy-denied endpoint is EXCLUDED from the consensus vote, the same treatment an unreachable endpoint already received in this module's own pre-existing design (never counted as dissent). All-denied degrades to invoke:null, the same 'nothing to call' path a missing endpoint always produced. resolveLlmInvokeWithDecision returns a new decisions array (full per-endpoint detail) alongside a single aggregate decision (first denial, or the first result) so the two pre-existing callers (hunter.js, disprove.js), which only ever read .reason in the all-null case, keep working unmodified.

isLoopbackUrl (the mechanism mode:local-only relies on, in llm-validator/local-endpoint.js) was separately, adversarially tested against known real-world localhost-bypass techniques rather than trusted from its own design comments: octal/hex/decimal/short-form IPv4 notations for 127.0.0.1 (e.g. http://0x7f.0.0.1/) are all correctly recognized as loopback — confirmed this is SAFE, not a smuggling hole, because Node's WHATWG-compliant URL parser canonicalizes these to the literal string "127.0.0.1" BEFORE the regex ever runs, verified directly by printing new URL(...).hostname for each case. Hostname lookalikes (localhost.evil.com, 127.0.0.1.nip.io, uppercase EVIL.COM), IPv4-mapped IPv6 forms, and URL-parsing userinfo-confusion tricks (user:pass@127.0.0.1@evil.com) are all correctly rejected.

Updated egress/policy.js's own module header (which had explicitly flagged FR-605 as 'still local-only-preset scoped' future work) to reflect the current, verified reality: mode:local-only is in scope and enforced across every real caller, with the one gap found and closed documented inline rather than left stale.

Deliberately did NOT attempt a call-site-level automated guard for this specific gap class (a file-level completeness check, egress-policy-completeness.test.js, already exists but is coarse — it checks 'does this file import evaluateEgress at all', which would NOT have caught this bug since discovery/llm-invoke.js already imported evaluateEgress, just didn't call it for one specific branch). Building a call-site-level AST checker is a larger undertaking flagged as remaining work, not attempted opportunistically within this cycle's scope.
tests: scanner/test/local-only-mode.test.js (new, 9 tests, registered in test:discovery matching its actual subject): isLoopbackUrl adversarial cases (alternate IPv4 notations correctly recognized via parser normalization; hostname lookalikes rejected; userinfo confusion rejected; unparseable/non-http(s) input fails closed). FR-605 regression: mode:local-only denies EVERY endpoint in a 2-remote-URL consensus list (this test would have FAILED against the pre-fix code, since the old consensus invoker was constructed unconditionally whenever ANY endpoints were configured); mode:local-only allows a MIXED list where the loopback endpoint survives and the remote one is excluded (proving per-endpoint exclusion, not all-or-nothing denial); mode:deny denies a consensus list even of loopback endpoints (proving deny is a blanket rule, not local-only-specific); default-allow policy still constructs a working consensus invoker (backward compatible); an injected llmInvoke callback still bypasses egress entirely, unchanged (the deliberate, documented escape hatch for test/consumer-supplied callbacks).

All pre-existing egress/discovery tests (discovery-llm-invoke.test.js 5, egress-policy-completeness.test.js 3, egress-policy.test.js and egress-policy-integration.test.js totaling 21) pass unchanged — 29 tests total, zero regressions from the fix.

FR-606.title: Surface model unavailability or refusal without converting it into a clean deterministic conclusion
evidence: Investigation (continuing the E5/E7/E8/E9 survey, natural continuation of FR-605's egress-path tracing through llm-validator/index.js) traced every degrade branch in validateOne/validateMany and found EVERY ONE of them set the SAME finding.validator_verdict ('unvalidated'), with the actual reason scattered across an inconsistently-populated free-text field (_validatorError: 'egress-policy-denied' | 'cost-ceiling' | 'HTTP 500' | an arbitrary exception message | ...completely UNSET for the 'nothing configured at all' case, confirmed by direct code read — the !cfg branch never touched _validatorError at all before this fix). A reader had no reliable, closed-vocabulary way to answer 'did the model tier even run, and if not, why' — exactly the gap FR-606's acceptance criterion names by requiring 5 specific, distinguishable states.

scanner/src/llm-validator/model-status.js (new): MODEL_STATUS defines EXACTLY the 5 values the PRD names verbatim (model-disabled, policy-blocked, unavailable, malformed, completed) as a frozen object, so a 6th ad-hoc string can never silently appear. summarizeModelStatus(findings) aggregates per-finding status into scan-level counts plus a notApplicable bucket for findings genuinely outside the taxonomy (see next point) — never silently folding a 'not applicable' case into one of the 5.

Precise mapping to every real branch in llm-validator/index.js's validateOne/validateMany, each independently proven by a test that reproduces the REAL condition (env config / mocked fetch / mocked response shape), not just asserted from reading the code: DISABLED = nothing configured at all, OR an explicit operator opt-out (AGENTIC_SECURITY_LLM_VALIDATE=0); POLICY_BLOCKED = the local preset's own loopback-only refusal (distinguished from DISABLED via the pre-existing _localPresetRefusal side-channel, which the module already used for a DIFFERENT report field), an egress-policy denial (FR-601), a cost-ceiling cap (valid or malformed config), or a network-level exception during validateOne itself; UNAVAILABLE = the endpoint was reached and attempted but failed (non-2xx HTTP status or a fetch/network exception inside callEndpoint); MALFORMED = a 2xx response came back but its content could not be parsed/verified into a usable answer (challenge/nonce cross-check failure, unparseable JSON); COMPLETED = a real validated verdict, INCLUDING a cache hit (the model answered at some point; not re-asking is an optimization, not a different outcome — proven by a dedicated test that a cache hit produces COMPLETED, not a sixth ad-hoc status).

Deliberately NOT stamped for findings skipped for reasons unrelated to model availability — an SCA locator with no line number, or a finding with no precise file:line at all. Forcing these into the 5-state taxonomy would misrepresent a finding-SUITABILITY question as a model-AVAILABILITY one; both already have their own honest verdict ('not-applicable' / 'unvalidated' with a distinct _validatorError), and this fix is additive, not a replacement for that existing signal. Proven by a dedicated test.

Own test-infrastructure bug found and fixed during verification, not a product bug: the first draft of the cache-hit test failed because the scan root (a bare mkdtempSync directory) had no project marker, so state-dir.js's isSafeStateDir silently refused the disk cache write — the SAME historical bug this codebase's own state-dir.js comment already documents ('the validator cache never persisted a single entry').
