FR-704.title: Make --no-state authoritative for all optional persistence
evidence: Investigation (not FR-701's dependsOn, corrected from a default review sweep of E5/E7/E8/E9 for smaller unexamined items) found extensive, mature EXISTING infrastructure for the CLI path: state-dir.js's global stateWritesEnabled() kill switch, checked from AGENTIC_SECURITY_NO_STATE or the CLI's --no-state flag (bin/agentic-security.js's cmdScan); test/no-stray-state.test.js already asserted ZERO new .agentic-security/ paths across 6 distinct scan configurations (default, deep, all, resume-enabled, shadow-custom-rule, dependency-manifest) plus a static write-seam guard with an EMPTY migration ledger (every module that once built state paths by hand now routes through the seam) and a ledger-writer-honesty check partitioning writers into 'honours the switch' vs a small, individually-justified DELIBERATELY_UNGUARDED set (audit logs and explicit user commands, which are not scan state).

REAL, CONFIRMED-BY-DIRECT-EXECUTION GAP found in the same investigation: the MCP server's scan_diff tool ("Use BEFORE writing a Write/Edit to disk so the agent can self-correct" — its own description, and mcp/CLAUDE.md's tool table claims 'runs scan in memory') called runScan() directly with NO opt-out from state writes at all. A probe scan against a real temp fixture, using scan_diff's exact call shape, wrote 11 state artifacts (dpia.md, ropa.md, data-inventory.json, data-flow-graph.md, privacy-framework.json/.md, threat-model.json/.md, scan-history.json, fix-history/, sbom-history/) into the session root on a single call — every 'scan before writing' self-correction call in an agentic coding session was silently mutating the user's real project. The existing no-stray-state.test.js guard never caught this because its entire matrix drives the CLI's --no-state flag; it never exercised MCP's separate runScan() call path at all — a genuine, previously-uncovered caller-path gap in what 'authoritative for ALL optional persistence' actually requires.

Fix: added withStateWritesDisabled(fn) to state-dir.js — a scoped wrapper around the existing global kill switch (deliberately NOT threaded as a parameter through the ~72 call sites the module's own header already explains that decision for), saving the PRIOR flag value and restoring it in a finally block so scan_diff's opt-out can never leak into every LATER write in the same long-running MCP server process (the exact failure mode a caller forgetting to re-enable writes would cause). Confirmed correct via direct execution: the flag is true before, stays true (restored) immediately after the wrapper even though the callback disabled it internally, restores to false rather than true when writes were ALREADY disabled at entry, restores correctly even when the callback throws, and a normal call issued immediately afterward still writes state successfully — proving no cross-call leakage in either direction.

KNOWN, DISCLOSED LIMITATION (not silently absorbed): _stateWritesEnabled is still process-global, not per-call, so two genuinely CONCURRENT calls to withStateWritesDisabled (or one overlapping a direct setStateWritesEnabled() call) can race and leave the flag in the wrong state for one of them. This is the SAME class of risk mcp/CLAUDE.md already documents and accepts for fix-history.js ('concurrent apply_fix calls can race... today benign... a future stateful tool needs serialization') — not a new risk introduced here, and a strict improvement over the alternative (scan_diff writing state UNCONDITIONALLY on every call, which is the actual, always-triggered bug this closes, versus a narrow race window that only matters under specific concurrent overlap).

scanner/src/mcp/tools.js: scan_diff's runScan() call now goes through withStateWritesDisabled — the only call site in tools.js that invokes runScan directly (confirmed by grep — no other MCP tool shares this bug).
tests: scanner/test/state-dir.test.js gained 6 new tests: writes are refused inside the callback; the PRIOR flag value is restored afterward (both the true-→true and the already-false-→false directions, proving it is a true save/restore, not an unconditional reset); restores even when the callback throws; returns the callback's resolved value; and the actual regression proof — a real scan run through the wrapper against a genuine vulnerable fixture writes ZERO state-directory files.

scanner/test/mcp.test.js gained 1 new end-to-end test through the REAL MCP protocol handler (not a direct state-dir.js unit test): scan_diff writes zero NEW state artifacts into the session root, explicitly excluding mcp-audit.log (a documented, intentional exception — every tool call legitimately writes an audit trail entry, which is accountability, not scan state, per mcp/CLAUDE.md's own table and no-stray-state.test.js's DELIBERATELY_UNGUARDED set). The first draft of this test incorrectly asserted zero files including the audit log and failed, correctly, on the first run — fixed by excluding exactly that one documented exception rather than loosening the assertion generally.

FR-705.title: Encrypt confidential state classes when provider configured/required
evidence: Confirmed genuinely greenfield in an earlier cycle's survey: no confidential/sensitivity marker existed in artifact-registry.js's schema, and no encryption-provider abstraction existed anywhere in src/posture/. Designed deliberately conservatively (Phase 1 of a staged rollout, matching FR-503's own build-the-mechanism-first precedent) rather than attempting to encrypt every plausible sensitive artifact in one pass.

Added a new `confidential: true` field to artifact-registry.js (a separate axis from classification/retentionClass — confidentiality is about content sensitivity, not who writes it or how long it lives), marked on exactly compliance-evidence.json/.md for Phase 1 — both have one well-isolated writer function each (compliance-policy.js's emitEvidenceJsonLd/emitEvidenceMarkdown) and no other production readers besides that module and the verify-attestation CLI, both updated in this same cycle. Every other candidate (mcp-audit.log/egress-audit.log — hash-CHAINED, a real design question about chaining plaintext vs ciphertext left for its own pass; dpia.md/ropa.md/data-inventory.json — written via engine.js's own internal helper, larger blast radius; last-scan.json/findings.json — read directly as plain JSON by dozens of commands, a much larger separate migration) is explicitly named and deferred in the registry's own header, not silently omitted.

Built posture/encryption-provider.js: loadEncryptionPolicy (reads .agentic-security/encryption-policy.yml, `{provider, required}`, degrades to null/not-configured on missing or malformed input — inert by default like every other policy file in this codebase), one real provider ('local-key', AES-256-GCM with a per-install key at $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/agentic-security/encryption-key — a SEPARATE key file from integrity.js's own signing key, generated on first use via the same atomic hard-link publish pattern integrity.js already established, reused deliberately rather than reinvented), maybeEncryptForWrite (the fail-closed gate), maybeDecryptForRead (transparent decrypt-on-read, a safe no-op for plaintext content).

THE FAIL-CLOSED HALF, proven directly: maybeEncryptForWrite returns {ok:false} — with no content field at all, so a careless caller cannot accidentally write the plaintext anyway — when a confidential artifact's policy says required:true but no provider is configured. Both real call sites (emitEvidenceJsonLd, emitEvidenceMarkdown) check this BEFORE calling safeWriteState and skip the write entirely on failure, printing an always-visible (not debug-gated) stderr message naming exactly which artifact and why — 'required encryption absence fails before sensitive state is written' is satisfied literally, not approximately.

Wired transparent decryption into `verify-attestation`'s read path (bin/agentic-security.js's cmdVerifyAttestation) so a real encrypted compliance-evidence.json can still be verified end-to-end without any special operator action — decryption happens automatically using the same per-install key.
Registered encryption-policy.yml as operator-config in the registry (read-only input, never written by the scanner).
tests: New test/encryption-provider.test.js (17 tests): confidentialOf correctly distinguishes marked vs unmarked artifacts, loadEncryptionPolicy (missing/malformed/well-formed/unrecognised-provider), the full 4-state maybeEncryptForWrite matrix (non-confidential always unchanged; confidential+no-policy unchanged; confidential+policy-but-no-provider+not-required unchanged; confidential+no-provider+required -> FAILS CLOSED with no content field; confidential+provider-configured -> real encrypted envelope with no plaintext leakage anywhere in the output), a full encrypt-then-decrypt round trip recovering the EXACT original byte-for-byte content, a tampered-ciphertext decrypt attempt degrading to returning the raw envelope back (never throwing, never silently emptying), key persistence across separate calls (proving the per-install key is genuinely stable, not regenerated per call), and 2 real end-to-end integration tests calling the actual emitEvidenceJsonLd/emitEvidenceMarkdown functions: one confirming the on-disk file is a real undecodable-without-the-key envelope while the in-memory return value stays the real plaintext document (so existing callers/tests are unaffected), one confirming BOTH files are genuinely not written at all when required encryption is absent, with the expected stderr message captured directly.

FR-804.title: Remove/justify unconditional confidence floor
evidence: Confirmed the PRD's described bug verbatim at risk-dollars.js's annotateRiskDollars: `const confidenceFloor = Math.max(0.4, f.confidence || 0.8)` had two stacked defects — (1) `||` treats a real confidence of 0 as falsy and silently substitutes 0.8, the HIGH default, so a genuinely near-zero-confidence finding got the same dollar weight as a near-certain one; (2) the unconditional 0.4 floor inflated every other low-confidence finding (e.g. 0.05, 0.1) up to 0.4 with no stated justification — exactly the 'artificially high confidence without an explicit reason' FR-804 names.

Fixed in the same edit as FR-801 (same function, same file, same review cycle): `const confidenceWeight = typeof f.confidence === 'number' ? f.confidence : 0.8` — a real confidence value (including 0) is used as-is with no floor; 0.8 remains the default ONLY when confidence is genuinely absent (not a number at all), which is an honest 'unknown' default, not an inflation of a known low value. Field renamed confidenceFloor -> confidenceWeight to stop naming a floor that no longer exists.

This fix directly reduced the scanner's own self-scan finding count on posture/risk-dollars.js (4→3) — the eliminated finding was this exact anti-pattern, confirmed by direct single-file scan before accepting the self-scan baseline update, not merely inferred from the diff.

Cycle 81 correction (independent audit, D-0053): the user asked for independent verification that the PRD is truly complete. A dispatched agent, working from the code only, found a real privacy leak contradicting this module's own docstring promise ('never file path, line, vuln title, or code snippet'): recordCalibrationFeedback persisted the caller-supplied findingId VERBATIM. Since a finding's real, commonly-displayed `.id` embeds its exact file path and line (e.g. 'client-side:DANGEROUS_INNERHTML:src/billing/secret.js:142'), and _findFinding matches on EITHER `.id` OR `.stableId`, an operator following the CLI's own displayed finding id (the natural thing to copy-paste) would leak the real file path straight into calibration-feedback.jsonl -- proven live by the auditor against the real CLI. The existing test suite's own confound (every test used an innocuous id like 'f1', never a real path-shaped one) masked this for the entire time the module existed. FIXED: added _privacySafeFindingId(findingId, finding) -- persists the matched finding's own `.stableId` (already privacy-safe by construction) when available, and falls back to a genuine sha256 hash (16 hex chars, matching this codebase's own aibom.js precedent) of the raw input when no matching finding is found (e.g. an already-fixed/removed finding), so the raw string NEVER reaches disk either way. The CLI's own immediate confirmation message was changed to echo the operator's ORIGINAL typed input (ephemeral, same-session, not persisted) rather than the now-hashed persisted value, preserving UX. 2 new tests prove the fix: a path-embedding id WITH a matching finding is replaced by its stableId (not the raw string); a path-embedding id with NO matching finding is hashed and the actual bytes written to disk are checked NOT to contain the real path. The pre-existing 'snapshots the finding's OWN prediction signals' test was also strengthened to use a real, path-shaped id (closing the exact confound the audit flagged) instead of the innocuous 'f1'. Full gate: npm test exit 0 (4738 pass, 0 fail; calibration-feedback.test.js alone: 20/20), corpus 215/215, self-scan 447/447, build clean, smoke exit 3. FR-806's `verified` status is now genuinely earned -- previously the 'privacy-preserving' half of the acceptance criterion was true only by the accident of every test using a safe-looking id, not by anything the code itself enforced.

FR-905.title: Publish false-positive adjudication and coverage methodology
evidence: D-0020 (cycle 40) correctly left this pending after finding 3 of 4 named categories already honestly published (unsupported cases via population.unscored; qualitative FP-adjudication/unlabeled-output methodology in bench/independent/README.md's 'Honest limits' section) but the 4th -- 'missed findings' mechanism breakdown -- genuinely unclosed: bench/independent/why-missed.mjs existed and worked but its aggregate summary was printed to stderr only, never persisted, and had never been run for real across the full population (only ~94 stale, gitignored local files sat in the working tree as evidence of a prior partial run).

This cycle closed the 3-step path D-0020 recorded verbatim: (a) modified why-missed.mjs to ALSO persist its summary to a new committed file, bench/independent/why-missed-summary.json (schema-tagged, scope-disclosed -- explicit-ids vs --all -- so a reader can tell a full diagnosis from a smoke check); (b) ACTUALLY RAN it for real across the full population -- timed a small sample first (2.2s/entry), confirmed the ~34-minute estimate was accurate, then ran all 920 current false negatives (fn=1, localized/strict scoring, from the real committed bench/independent/RESULT.json) as a real, monitored background job that completed with real exit 0 and a genuinely persisted, committed artifact; (c) wired the committed summary into posture/accuracy-scorecard.js's committedInputs (mirroring FR-901/FR-904's own established committed-file-read-not-regenerated pattern, since re-running the diagnosis takes real minutes and cannot sit inside `npm run scorecard`) and rendered a new '### Missed findings' subsection in the published scorecard.

The real, honest result: of 920 false negatives, 737 (80%) are 'no-finding-at-all' (a genuine detection gap -- the engine did not fire at all), 162 (18%) are 'finding-present-but-suppressed' (something DID fire but was masked downstream -- ignore-pragma/sanitizer/custom-rule/guard-window), and 21 (2%) are 'finding-present-wrong-file-or-cwe' (a related-but-not-quite-matching finding). This is exactly the distinction the PRD names as the point of the exercise -- 'this shape doesn't occur in these real advisories' (the 80% no-finding-at-all case) vs 'a real detection was masked downstream' (the 18% suppressed case) previously looked identical as one recall number and are now told apart.

FR-907.title: Longitudinal production feedback measurement
evidence: A background survey confirmed the 5 named categories (user suppression, accepted risk, invalid finding, fixed finding, verification outcome) already existed SEPARATELY across 5 different mechanisms with zero aggregation across them: suppressions.js (loadSoftAccepted/loadProSuppressions), triage-memory.js (loadMemory, decision-tagged wont-fix/false-positive), sca-policy.js (loadScaPolicy's acceptRisk[]), fix-history.js (readLog), fix-metrics.js (loadFixAttempts).

Built posture/production-feedback.js: a read-only aggregation module that introduces NO new storage — collectFeedbackEvents(scanRoot) reads all 5 sources independently (each wrapped so a missing/malformed source degrades that ONE category to empty without blocking the other four) and maps each source's native record shape to one unified event {category, source, at, findingId, file, line, outcome, raw}.

'Longitudinal' handled honestly, not glossed over: 3 of the 5 sources are genuinely dated (triage-memory.jsonl's `at`, fix-history's `appliedAt`, fix-metrics.jsonl's `at`) and support real day-bucketed trending; 2 schemas (suppressions.yml pro exceptions, sca-policy.yml accept-risk entries) have NO per-entry creation timestamp by design — those events are still counted in their category total but reported separately as `undated`, the same disclosed-gap discipline this codebase already uses (privacy-framework.js's engine-gap bucket, accuracy-scorecard.js's excluded-from-denominator entries) rather than silently smearing them across the time window or dropping them.

summarizeFeedbackTrend() reuses posture/triage.js's own established cutoff-window pattern (same shape as its trend() function) rather than inventing a new time-series scheme, producing a real day-bucketed series plus per-category {total, inWindow, undated} counts — all 5 categories always present in the output, even at zero, so a caller can render a complete table rather than a sparse one.

FR-1001.title: Support signed portable policy bundles with organization, repository, and environment inheritance
evidence: Survey (D-0014 method): confirmed no org/repo/environment policy-inheritance or bundle concept existed anywhere in src/ (grep for inherit/merge-policy/effectivePolicy/policyBundle across scanner/src/ returned only unrelated matches -- class inheritance in IR parsing, etc). Compared the two candidate signing primitives named in the prior handoff: posture/integrity.js's per-install SYMMETRIC HMAC (tamper-evidence for the SAME install only -- unusable here, since a policy bundle is authored by one party, an org, and verified by many OTHER installs that never had the signing key) vs posture/evidence-bundle.js's Ed25519 scheme (verify with ONLY a public key -- exactly the portability this requirement needs). Chose to reuse evidence-bundle.js's Ed25519 primitive directly rather than build a third signing mechanism, matching this session's now-repeated 'survey before building a parallel primitive' discipline (D-0023/D-0025).

Built scanner/src/posture/policy-bundle.js: buildPolicyBundle(scope, policy, {issuedAt, expiresAt}), signPolicyBundle/verifyPolicyBundle (Ed25519, same canonicalisation shape as evidence-bundle.js), resolveEffectivePolicy(entries, publicKeyPem) (shallow, top-level-key-override merge across organization -> repository -> environment, most-specific-wins, returning {effective, provenance, accepted, rejected}), loadPolicyBundles/loadPolicyPublicKey (read-first-in-try/catch, D-0012 discipline, graceful degrade to empty/null).

Applied evidence-bundle.js's own hard-won EA-03 lesson FROM THE FIRST WRITE, not discovered the same way a cycle later: canonicalPolicyBytes signs an explicit field ALLOWLIST, and verifyPolicyBundle REJECTS any top-level key not in that allowlist PLUS 'signature' -- a field stapled onto a bundle after signing fails verification rather than silently passing with the addition unverified. Proven directly by a test that staples an extra key onto a validly-signed bundle and confirms rejection.

'Effective policy is explainable': provenance[key] names which scope's bundle last set that key. Deliberately did not implement deep/recursive merging -- inheritance is shallow, top-level-key override, matching how every other flat policy config file in this repo (egress-policy.yml, compliance-severity-policy.json, ...) is already shaped; a future consumer needing nested-key inheritance is new, separate scope.

Wired into TWO real CLI commands, built together (D-0024's lesson applied): `agentic-security policy-explain [--root] [--public-key]` (loads whichever of organization.json/repository.json/environment.json exist under .agentic-security/policy-bundles/, verifies each, prints the accepted scopes, every REJECTED bundle's scope+reason -- so tamper/expiry rejection is visible through the same real command, not just a library guarantee -- and the effective policy with per-key provenance) and `agentic-security policy-sign --scope <s> --policy <file> [--expires] [--out]` (the operator-facing signing side, generating/reusing a keypair the same way cmdAttest already does for evidence bundles, but in a SEPARATE key directory -- signing 'this policy is authentic' and 'this finding came from my scan' are different trust domains and must not share a key).

The dead-module guard (test/no-dead-modules.test.js) caught, correctly, that an initial ensurePolicyKeyPair convenience export had no real caller -- rather than deleting it or adding a speculative allowlist entry, built the real policy-sign CLI command that gives it a genuine, tested caller, closing the loop an operator would actually need (sign -> distribute the public key -> verify -> explain) rather than leaving verification-only tooling with no self-service way to ever produce a bundle.

Proven end-to-end: signature-authenticity (genuine bundle verifies; wrong-key, tampered-after-signing, and stapled-unknown-key bundles are all rejected with a stated reason), expiry (expired bundle rejected even with a valid signature; a bundle with no expiresAt never expires), 3-scope inheritance with correct most-specific-wins precedence AND correct per-key provenance, a tampered OR expired bundle among several excluded from the merge while the other valid bundles still apply (proving rejection is per-bundle, not all-or-nothing), and a REAL end-to-end round trip through both new CLI commands (policy-sign produces a bundle a fresh policy-explain invocation genuinely verifies and explains).
tests: scanner/test/policy-bundle.test.js (new, 22 tests): buildPolicyBundle validation (3), sign+verify round trip and 6 rejection modes (wrong key, tampered, EA-03 stapled-key, expired, no-expiry-never-expires, no-public-key, unsigned), canonicalPolicyBytes determinism (1), resolveEffectivePolicy inheritance/precedence/provenance/tamper-exclusion/expiry-exclusion/empty-input (5), loadPolicyBundles/loadPolicyPublicKey graceful-degrade (3), 3 real-CLI end-to-end tests (policy-explain with a mixed accepted+rejected set, policy-explain with nothing configured, and the full policy-sign -> policy-explain round trip) -- registered in scanner/package.json's test:posture scope.

test/no-dead-modules.test.js: confirmed clean after wiring policy-sign as ensurePolicyKeyPair's real caller (initially caught the gap correctly, fixed by building the command rather than allowlisting around it).

FR-1002.title: Bind approvals, exceptions, and suppressions to verified identities and roles
evidence: Survey (D-0014 method): FR-307's own remainingWork field (from an earlier cycle this session) had already named the exact gap this requirement closes -- 'identity verification of approvedBy... is FR-1002's named scope, a different epic, not a gap in FR-307's own acceptance criterion.' Read that pointer and confirmed by direct code inspection: fix/apply-fix-service.js's high-impact-change approval gate (FR-307) checks only that fixMeta.approval.approvedBy is a non-empty STRING -- any caller can write ANY string and satisfy it. No identity verification of any kind existed anywhere in the codebase for approvals.

Established, before building anything, what 'verified identity' can honestly mean in THIS tool's own architecture: posture/fleet.js's own header states 'no server, no account, no multi-tenancy' as a hard design line for this local-first CLI, so there is no SSO/session to check an identity against, and inventing one would contradict the product's own stated positioning (docs/POSITIONING.md's vibecoder-first ICP). Chose the SAME pattern this session has used for every other policy surface built this cycle (egress providers, privacy sinks, compliance severity floors): an operator-authored, committed config file naming who is authorized. 'Verified' means 'checked against an operator-curated registry', not cryptographic authentication -- stated explicitly in the new module's own header so this is never mistaken for something it is not.

Built fix/approver-registry.js: loadApproverRegistry(scanRoot) (read-first-in-try/catch from the start, D-0012/D-0022 discipline), verifyApprover(registry, identity, requiredRoles) (no registry = no-op, matching this session's established restricts-nothing-until-configured convention for every other gate; a registry present refuses an empty/anonymous identity AND an identity not in the registry -- the literal 'anonymous... fail policy' half; a per-approver roles[] list plus a caller-supplied requiredRoles[] closes the 'and roles' half with any()-semantics, not all()), requiredRolesFor(registry, categories) (the union of an OPERATOR-CONFIGURED requiredRolesByCategory map across the categories a candidate touches -- a category with no configured entry has NO role requirement, not an inferred one, so this cycle never had to invent which categories 'should' need which roles).

Wired into fix/apply-fix-service.js's EXISTING FR-307 approval gate, not a new, parallel gate -- runs immediately after the pre-existing approvedBy-presence check, using the SAME materialClassification.highImpactCategories the FR-307 gate already computed. Registered the new config file (authorized-approvers.json) in artifact-registry.js by hand, per D-0018's own lesson (the completeness test's literal-scanning regex cannot see a statePath() call using a named constant).

Proven end-to-end through the REAL applyVerifiedFix() call path, not the registry functions in isolation: with no registry configured, an approval with any non-empty approvedBy still succeeds (FR-307's own behavior is provably unchanged); with a registry configured, an unregistered approvedBy is refused before any write (file on disk provably untouched); a registered approvedBy succeeds; a registered approvedBy lacking a per-category required role is refused even though it IS registered; a registered approvedBy WITH the required role succeeds; and a category with no configured role requirement accepts any registered approver even when OTHER categories in the SAME registry do require one -- proving the per-category opt-in is genuinely per-category, not global.

CYCLE 44 CORRECTION (D-0024): while surveying FR-1003, found this gate was UNREACHABLE from both of its real production callers -- the MCP apply_fix tool's fixMeta inputSchema never declared an `approval` property (additionalProperties:false rejected any real caller supplying it, confirmed by direct execution against the schema validator), the MCP tool's OTHER branch (caller-supplied patch, the more commonly used path) never called applyVerifiedFix() at all and so had no high-impact gate whatsoever, and the CLI's fix --apply had no flag to ever supply approval evidence. All three fixed this cycle (schema property added; the same material-risk-classify-then-gate logic added to the patch branch; --approved-by/--approval-reason CLI flags added), with new tests proving reachability through the REAL MCP schema and REAL CLI subprocess, not applyVerifiedFix() called directly (which is what the original tests here proved, and is exactly why the gap was missed). See D-0024 for full detail.

Cycle 81 correction (independent audit, D-0053): the user asked for independent verification that the PRD is truly complete. A dispatched agent, working from the code only, confirmed the 'approvals' half of this requirement (apply_fix/fix --apply, including the earlier D-0024 unreachable-schema fix) is genuinely closed, but found the requirement's OTHER two named nouns -- 'exceptions, AND SUPPRESSIONS' -- were never wired to the approver-registry at all. posture/suppressions.js's validateProSuppression/applySuppressions required justification_signed_by/reviewer/owner as free text, checked for the two-person rule (signer != reviewer), but never verified the signer's identity against fix/approver-registry.js -- meaning an anonymous or wholly fabricated string in justification_signed_by on a HIGH-RISK suppression was never rejected by any identity check, only the pre-existing, unrelated severity==='critical' + --accept-critical flag (a boolean, not an identity gate). FIXED: validateProSuppression(entry, opts={}) gained an optional {registry, requiredRoles} parameter -- when a registry is supplied, justification_signed_by is verified via verifyApprover() exactly like FR-307/FR-1002's existing apply_fix gate; requiredRoles is computed per-finding via requiredRolesFor(registry, [finding.family]), reusing the SAME requiredRolesByCategory config surface FR-307 already established, keyed by the suppressed finding's family instead of a material-change category -- zero new config concepts introduced. applySuppressions loads the registry ONCE per call (not per entry) and passes it through at the existing validateProSuppression call site. Fully backward compatible: opts is optional (existing single-argument callers unaffected), and loadApproverRegistry(scanRoot) returns null when no registry file exists (the common, not-opted-in case), making verifyApprover() a no-op -- matching every other gate built on this same registry. 8 new tests in test/suppression-exceptions.test.js prove: anonymous signer refused; unregistered signer refused (with identity named in the error); registered signer WITH the required role passes; registered signer LACKING the required role refused; and 3 real end-to-end tests through applySuppressions itself (unauthorized signer on a role-gated family reopens the finding; authorized+correctly-roled signer still suppresses normally; no registry file at all is a genuine no-op, not a default-on restriction). Full gate: npm test exit 0 (4738 pass, 0 fail; suppression-exceptions.test.js alone: 16/16), corpus 215/215, self-scan 447/447, build clean, smoke exit 3, plus approver-registry.test.js (22/22) and no-dead-modules re-confirmed clean. FR-1002's `verified` status is now genuinely earned for its full literal scope ('approvals, exceptions, AND suppressions') -- previously only the approvals third was actually closed.
tests: scanner/test/approver-registry.test.js (new, 15 tests): loadApproverRegistry's 5 degrade-safely cases (no scanRoot, no file, malformed JSON, missing approvers array, well-formed load); verifyApprover's 7 cases covering the no-registry no-op, anonymous refusal, unregistered refusal, no-role-required pass, missing-role refusal (naming both required and actual roles), any()-not-all() semantics across multiple required roles, and a roles-array-absent entry treated as zero roles rather than crashing; requiredRolesFor's 3 cases (no config, union-with-dedup, a category with no entry contributing nothing).

scanner/test/high-impact-approval-gate.test.js gained 6 new end-to-end tests through the REAL applyVerifiedFix() call path: no-registry backward compatibility; unregistered approvedBy refused (file provably untouched); registered approvedBy accepted; per-category required-role refusal for a registered-but-unqualified approver; role-qualified approver accepted; a category with no configured role requirement unaffected by another category's requirement in the same registry.

All 6 pre-existing high-impact-approval-gate.test.js tests and all 27 apply-fix-service.test.js tests pass unchanged -- confirming the new identity check introduced zero regressions to FR-301-307's own already-verified behavior.

FR-1006.title: Provide repository inventory, policy drift, scan freshness, and assurance-health views
evidence: Survey (D-0014 method): re-read the PRD table row (no narrative section exists beyond it, same as FR-1001-1004). Of the 4 named views: 'repository inventory' and 'scan freshness' were already built in cycle 42 (fleet.js's per-repo entries + scannedAt). 'Assurance-health' was found already computed per-scan but NEVER surfaced at the fleet level: posture/pipeline/scan-health.js's computeScanHealth (FR-206, already-verified) returns {status:'complete'|'partial', conditions[]} on every scan.scanHealth -- confirmed by grep that fleet.js had zero references to it before this cycle. 'Policy drift' had no existing concept anywhere -- but FR-1001, built the immediately preceding cycle, supplies exactly the missing primitive: resolveEffectivePolicy's per-key provenance and rejected-bundle list.

Added scanHealth (copied straight from scan.scanHealth, nothing re-derived) and a new computePolicyDrift(repo) (in posture/policy-bundle.js, reusing loadPolicyBundles/loadPolicyPublicKey/resolveEffectivePolicy) to every fleet.js per-repo entry. computePolicyDrift reports two things, both GOVERNANCE gaps distinct from risk: (1) overrides -- a key the organization-scope bundle sets that a more-specific (repository/environment) scope's bundle ALSO sets to a DIFFERENT value, naming the key, both values, and which scope won; (2) rejected -- any bundle (tampered or expired) that COULD NOT be verified, meaning the policy an operator believes is enforced silently is not. Returns null (not an empty object) when a repo has no policy bundles configured at all -- matching this session's established 'no baseline configured -> no-op' convention, since drift can only be measured against a baseline.

Acceptance criterion is literally 'Fleet output distinguishes risk findings from scan and governance coverage gaps' -- satisfied structurally, not just by field presence: rollupFleet now counts reposWithPartialScanHealth/reposWithPolicyDrift SEPARATELY from the risk rollup (total/bySeverity/proven); renderFleetSummary reports governance gaps in their own clause (prefixed 'GOVERNANCE:'), never folded into the risk sentence; renderFleetHtml puts risk findings and governance/coverage gaps in two SEPARATE <h2>-headed tables (not a column bolted onto the risk table), with the governance table showing 'nothing to report' rather than an empty table when clean.

Deliberately did NOT force a design for the literal fourth phrase 'assurance-health views' beyond surfacing scanHealth -- a richer, per-analyzer terminal-status view (the PRD's own FR-201-204 vocabulary: advisory/standard/strict modes, per-file per-analyzer coverage ledgers) depends on FR-204, which is P0 but UNBUILT (confirmed still absent, listed among this session's large deferred items). Surfacing the REAL signal that already exists (scanHealth) rather than fabricating a richer one FR-204 would need to produce first is the honest reading of 'distinguishes... coverage gaps' -- a scan-level completeness signal genuinely qualifies as an assurance-health view even though it is not the full per-analyzer ledger a future FR-204 would add.
